passages.q: Which parts of an apology matter most?
p: Public apologies from companies and leaders often seem to make things worse. Phrases like “we regret any inconvenience” or “mistakes were made” can sound evasive. Researchers have tried to identify what separates an apology that repairs trust from one that does not.

In a 2016 study, Roy Lewicki and colleagues tested six components of an apology: expressing regret, explaining what went wrong, acknowledging responsibility, declaring repentance, offering repair and requesting forgiveness. Participants rated apologies containing different combinations. Apologies with more components were judged more effective, but two stood out. Acknowledging responsibility mattered most, followed by an offer to repair the damage. Requesting forgiveness mattered least.

The finding fits everyday experience. An apology that names what you did and owns it signals that you understand the harm, and an offer to fix it shows you take it seriously. Explanations help, but if they sound like excuses they can backfire. For leaders, a useful test is whether the apology could be read aloud by the person harmed and feel accurate to them, rather than carefully protecting the person apologising.
g: Many public apologies sound evasive, so researchers studied what makes apologies repair trust.
A 2016 study found acknowledging responsibility mattered most, then offering repair, and asking forgiveness least.
Owning the harm and offering a fix signal understanding, so a good apology should feel accurate to the person harmed.
k: Evasive apologies can make things worse.
Of six components, acknowledging responsibility mattered most, then offering repair; asking forgiveness least.
Name and own the harm, offer to fix it, and avoid explanations that sound like excuses.

mc.s: What does the research suggest matters most in an apology?
mc.e: The second paragraph says acknowledging responsibility stood out most.

mc.e: The third paragraph warns about this.

v.d: Repentance is expressing remorse and a resolve not to repeat a wrong.

passages.q: Why do people consistently underestimate how long things will take?
p: The Sydney Opera House was expected to take about four years and cost around seven million Australian dollars. It took fourteen years and cost over a hundred million. Large projects running late and over budget are so common that Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky gave the tendency a name in 1979: the planning fallacy.

The fallacy arises because people plan from the inside view. They picture the specific steps of their own project and imagine them going roughly as intended. They underweight the many things that could go wrong, each unlikely on its own but likely in combination. Optimism, pressure to win approval and the desire to look capable all push estimates down. Strikingly, people make the same error even when they know that their previous projects ran late.

A remedy is to take the outside view. Instead of building an estimate from your plan’s details, ask how long similar projects actually took. This approach, called reference class forecasting, has been adopted for some public infrastructure planning. It feels less satisfying, because it ignores what is special about your project, but that is the point: most projects believe they are special, and most are late.
g: Projects like the Sydney Opera House ran far over time and budget, a tendency named the planning fallacy.
It happens because people plan from the inside view and underweight combined risks, even knowing past projects ran late.
So take the outside view and estimate from how long similar projects actually took.
k: Large projects routinely run late and over budget: the planning fallacy.
Inside-view planning underweights combined risks; optimism and pressure push estimates down.
Use the outside view: base estimates on how similar projects actually went.

o: Estimating from how similar projects actually performed
mc.e: The third paragraph recommends the outside view.

mc.s: Why do many small unlikely risks matter so much?

mc.e: The second paragraph says they are likely in combination.

passages.t: Food miles and the real footprint
passages.q: Is eating local the best way to cut food emissions?
p: Buying local food is often promoted as a way to reduce environmental impact, since food that travels shorter distances uses less fuel in transport. The idea is intuitive, and local food can have other benefits, such as supporting nearby farmers and freshness.

However, research comparing the full life cycle of foods tells a different story about emissions. A large 2018 study by Joseph Poore and Thomas Nemecek, analysing data from tens of thousands of farms, found that transport usually makes up only a small share of a food’s total greenhouse gas emissions, often under ten per cent. Most emissions come from land use and from what happens on the farm, such as methane from cattle and the clearing of forests for pasture. Air-freighted produce is a notable exception, since flying is very carbon-intensive.

The implication is that what you eat matters far more than where it comes from. Beef and lamb have much larger footprints than chicken, and plant foods such as beans and grains generally have far smaller footprints still, even when they travel long distances by ship. Local beef can have a much bigger impact than imported lentils. For someone wanting to cut emissions, changing the mix of foods does more than shortening the journey.
g: Local food is promoted as greener because of shorter transport, and it has other benefits too.
Life-cycle research shows transport is usually a small share of emissions, which mainly come from land use and farming, except air freight.
So what you eat matters far more than where it comes from, with beef and lamb far higher than plants.
k: Local food is promoted for shorter transport and other benefits.
Transport is usually under 10% of food emissions; land use and farming dominate (air freight is an exception).
What you eat matters more than where it’s from; local beef can exceed imported lentils.

o: The type of food matters more for emissions than how far it travels
Transport is the main source of food emissions

mc.e: The second paragraph notes air freight is very carbon-intensive.

passages.q: Can vertical farms feed cities?
p: Vertical farms grow crops indoors on stacked shelves under LED lights, with water and nutrients delivered by machines. Supporters highlight striking advantages: they can produce crops year-round regardless of weather, use far less water than fields, need no pesticides and can sit inside cities close to customers. Yields per square metre of floor space can be dozens of times higher than outdoor farming.

The catch is energy. Plants in fields get sunlight for free; indoor farms must replace it with electricity. Lighting and climate control make up a large share of costs, and when energy prices rose sharply in 2022, several well-funded vertical farming companies in Europe and the United States cut back or went bankrupt. The economics work best for high-value, fast-growing crops such as salad leaves and herbs, which are light and perishable.

Staple crops such as wheat, rice and potatoes, which provide most of the world’s calories, are poorly suited to vertical farms: they need lots of light, grow slowly and sell for low prices. Vertical farming may become a useful supplement for certain foods, especially where land is scarce or climates are harsh, but it is unlikely to replace fields for feeding the world.
g: Vertical farms grow crops indoors with year-round output, little water and very high yields per floor area.
But replacing sunlight with electricity is costly, so several firms failed when energy prices rose, and only high-value leafy crops pay.
Staple crops are poorly suited, so vertical farming may supplement but not replace fields.
k: Vertical farms offer year-round crops, low water use, no pesticides and high yields per area.
Energy for lighting is a major cost; several firms failed when prices rose; leafy greens suit best.
Staples are poorly suited; vertical farming may supplement, not replace, fields.

o: Vertical farming may supplement some foods but won’t replace fields

mc.e: The final sentence gives this conclusion.

passages.q: What gives a negotiator real power?
p: Many people enter negotiations focused on what they want: a salary, a price, a deadline. The negotiation experts Roger Fisher and William Ury, in their 1981 book Getting to Yes, argued that a more important number is what you will do if there is no deal. They called it your BATNA: the best alternative to a negotiated agreement.

Your BATNA defines your power. If you have a strong job offer elsewhere, you can afford to walk away from a weak one, and the other side will sense it. If your alternative is unemployment, you are more likely to accept poor terms. The same logic applies to the other party. Understanding their alternatives, and how attractive or unattractive they are, tells you how much room there is for a deal.

The practical advice is to improve your BATNA before negotiating, by developing real alternatives, and to know it clearly so that you neither accept a deal worse than it nor reject one that is better. Fisher and Ury also urged negotiators to focus on underlying interests rather than fixed positions. Two people arguing over an orange might both be satisfied if one wants the juice and the other the peel. A good alternative gives you the confidence to look for such solutions rather than grabbing the first offer.
g: Fisher and Ury argued the key number is what you will do without a deal: your BATNA.
Your BATNA defines your power, because strong alternatives let you walk away, and the other side’s shows the room for a deal.
So improve and know your BATNA, and focus on interests rather than positions to find better deals.
k: Your BATNA is the best alternative if no agreement is reached.
Strong alternatives give power; knowing the other side’s alternatives shows the room for a deal.
Improve your BATNA beforehand, know it clearly, and focus on interests, not positions.

o: The best alternative if no agreement is reached
The highest price you can ask
mc.e: The first paragraph defines it.

passages.q: Why did centrally planned economies struggle to work?
p: In the twentieth century, several countries tried to run their economies through central planning. Officials decided what factories should produce, in what quantities and at what prices. In principle, a wise planner could direct resources to where they were most needed, avoiding the waste and inequality of markets.

In 1945 the economist Friedrich Hayek published an essay, “The Use of Knowledge in Society”, explaining why this was so difficult. The knowledge needed to run an economy, he argued, is not concentrated anywhere. It is scattered among millions of people: a farmer’s knowledge of a field, a shopkeeper’s sense of what customers want this week, a factory manager’s awareness of a machine about to fail. No central office can gather all of this, and much of it is hard to put into words.

Prices, Hayek argued, solve this problem. When a material becomes scarce, its price rises, and people across the economy economise on it without needing to know why. Prices compress vast amounts of information into a signal anyone can act on. This does not mean markets are always right; they can fail, for example with pollution. But Hayek’s insight helps explain why planned economies so often produced shortages of some goods and gluts of others.
g: Central planning aimed to direct resources wisely by having officials set production and prices.
Hayek argued the needed knowledge is scattered among millions of people and often tacit, so no planner can gather it.
Prices transmit that information as signals, which explains planning’s shortages and gluts, though markets can still fail.
k: Planned economies had officials set production and prices.
Hayek (1945): economic knowledge is dispersed and often tacit; no centre can gather it.
Prices compress information into signals; planning led to shortages and gluts, though markets can fail.

o: Prices coordinate knowledge that is scattered across society

mc.e: The second and third paragraphs present this argument.

passages.q: Where does hydrogen make sense as a clean fuel?
p: Hydrogen is often presented as a clean fuel of the future. When it is burned or used in a fuel cell, the main by-product is water. If it is produced by splitting water using renewable electricity, so-called green hydrogen, the whole chain can be nearly emission-free. Governments and companies have announced large hydrogen strategies.

The difficulty is efficiency. Making hydrogen from electricity, compressing or liquefying it, transporting it and turning it back into energy loses a large share of the original electricity at each step. For a car, using the electricity directly in a battery is roughly two to three times more efficient than converting it to hydrogen first. Today, most hydrogen is actually made from natural gas, releasing carbon dioxide, which undermines its green image.

Hydrogen therefore makes most sense where direct electrification is hard. It is already a key ingredient in fertiliser production and oil refining, where cleaner hydrogen could cut emissions. It is being tested for steelmaking and could help fuel shipping or store energy for long periods. Analysts sometimes describe this as a hydrogen ladder: the uses at the top, where there are no good alternatives, deserve priority over those, such as home heating and cars, where batteries and heat pumps already work.
g: Hydrogen is promoted as clean because it produces water, and green hydrogen from renewables can be nearly emission-free.
But each conversion step wastes energy, so batteries are far more efficient for cars, and most hydrogen today comes from gas.
So hydrogen fits best where electrification is hard, such as fertiliser, steel and shipping, not cars or home heating.
k: Hydrogen produces water when used; green hydrogen from renewables can be near emission-free.
Conversion losses make it 2–3× less efficient than batteries for cars; most hydrogen today comes from gas.
Prioritise hard-to-electrify uses (fertiliser, steel, shipping, storage) over cars and home heating.

o: Hydrogen should be prioritised for uses that are hard to electrify

mc.e: The final paragraph sets out the hydrogen ladder.

passages.t: Do words shape what we see?
passages.q: Does the language you speak change how you think?
p: The idea that language shapes thought is often linked to Benjamin Lee Whorf, who argued in the mid-twentieth century that the structure of a language determines how its speakers perceive the world. In its strong form, the claim that people cannot think what their language cannot express has been largely abandoned. People can learn new concepts, and translation, though imperfect, is possible.

A weaker version has found support. Russian has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue. In a 2007 study, Russian speakers were slightly faster at telling apart two shades of blue when the shades fell on different sides of their language’s boundary, an advantage English speakers did not show. The effect disappeared when participants were given a verbal task to do at the same time, suggesting language was actively involved. Other studies suggest that languages that describe directions using north, south, east and west, rather than left and right, are linked to unusually good orientation.

The current view is that language does not imprison thought but can nudge it: drawing attention to some distinctions, making certain ideas easier to express and remember. This matters beyond linguistics. The words an organisation uses, such as calling customers “users” or problems “incidents”, can subtly shape what its people notice.
g: Whorf’s strong claim that language determines thought has been largely abandoned.
A weaker version has support: Russian speakers distinguish blues across their word boundary faster, and direction words link to orientation.
So language nudges rather than imprisons thought, which also applies to the words organisations use.
k: The strong idea that language determines thought has been abandoned.
Weaker effects exist: Russian blue distinctions, and cardinal-direction languages linked to orientation.
Language nudges attention and memory; organisational vocabulary can shape what people notice.

passages.q: Are mental shortcuts always a sign of poor thinking?
p: Much research on decision-making catalogues biases: ways in which shortcuts, or heuristics, lead people astray. Anchoring, overconfidence and confirmation bias are well documented. This work can leave the impression that intuitive thinking is generally faulty and that careful calculation is always better.

The psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer has argued for a different view, which he calls ecological rationality. Heuristics, he says, are often well suited to the environments people actually face, where time is short, information is incomplete and the future is uncertain. A simple rule can outperform complex analysis in such settings, because complex models tend to fit past noise rather than lasting patterns. Studies have found, for example, that simple rules for spreading investments evenly across options can perform as well as sophisticated optimisation methods when data are limited.

The two perspectives are not as opposed as they sometimes appear. Heuristics can fail badly in unfamiliar settings, such as statistical risks we rarely encounter, and work well in familiar, uncertain ones. The practical question is not whether to use shortcuts but which shortcuts fit which situations, and when it is worth slowing down to check.
g: Research on biases can suggest intuitive shortcuts are generally faulty.
Gigerenzer argues heuristics suit real uncertain environments, and simple rules can beat complex models that fit noise.
The views are compatible: the question is which shortcuts fit which situations and when to slow down.
k: Bias research shows heuristics can mislead.
Gigerenzer’s ecological rationality: simple rules often suit uncertain, information-poor environments and can beat complex models.
Shortcuts fail in unfamiliar settings and work in familiar ones; choose them to fit the situation.

passages.q: Why did growth in output per worker slow so sharply in Britain after 2008?
p: Productivity, the amount produced per hour worked, is the main driver of rising living standards over time. Before the 2008 financial crisis, British productivity grew at around two per cent a year. Afterwards, growth slowed dramatically, to well under one per cent for much of the following decade. Had the earlier trend continued, average incomes would now be substantially higher.

Economists have proposed many explanations. Banks weakened by the crisis may have kept weak firms alive while starving promising ones of credit. Low wages may have encouraged firms to hire workers rather than invest in machines and software. Uncertainty, including around Brexit, may have deterred investment. Some argue that productivity is being mismeasured, because free digital services are not well captured in output statistics, though most studies find this explains only a small part. The slowdown also hit many other rich countries, which suggests global factors such as slower spread of new technologies.

No single explanation dominates, and the causes probably combine. The puzzle matters because productivity determines what an economy can afford: wages, pensions and public services. It is why governments focus on investment, skills, infrastructure and helping new technologies spread from the best firms to the rest.
g: Productivity drives living standards, and UK growth fell from about 2% a year to under 1% after 2008.
Explanations include weak banks, cheap labour, uncertainty and mismeasurement, and similar slowdowns abroad suggest global causes.
Causes likely combine, and the puzzle matters because productivity sets what an economy can afford.
k: UK productivity growth fell from about 2% a year to well under 1% after 2008.
Possible causes: weak banks, cheap labour, uncertainty, mismeasurement (small), global technology diffusion.

passages.t: Do bike lanes hurt local shops?
passages.q: What happens to nearby businesses when parking is replaced by cycle lanes?
p: When a city proposes replacing roadside parking with a protected cycle lane, local shopkeepers are often among the fiercest opponents. Their reasoning is understandable: if customers cannot park outside, they may shop elsewhere. Surveys repeatedly find that retailers believe a larger share of their customers arrive by car than actually do.

Studies of real schemes, from New York to Toronto to several British cities, have generally found that retail activity on streets with new cycle lanes held steady or improved, though results vary by place and some individual businesses do lose out. One reason is that people arriving on foot or by bike tend to spend less per visit but visit more often, so over a month their spending can match or exceed that of drivers. Streets that are calmer and more pleasant may also encourage people to linger.

None of this means every scheme succeeds. Deliveries, access for disabled customers and the needs of businesses selling bulky goods require careful design, and disruption during construction can hurt. But the evidence suggests that the fear of commercial collapse is often based on an overestimate of how many customers drive, and that measuring actual customer behaviour before deciding is better than relying on impressions.
g: Shopkeepers often oppose cycle lanes, overestimating how many customers arrive by car.
Studies generally find retail held steady or improved, partly because walkers and cyclists visit more often.
Some schemes need careful design, but fears often rest on overestimates, so measure actual behaviour before deciding.
k: Retailers overestimate how many customers drive.
Studies generally find retail holds steady or improves; walkers and cyclists visit more often.

passages.t: Um, uh and the art of pausing
passages.q: Are filler words like “um” always a sign of poor speaking?
p: Public speaking advice often treats “um” and “uh” as faults to eliminate. Listeners do notice them, and frequent fillers can make a speaker sound less prepared. Yet fillers appear in the speech of nearly everyone, in every language, which suggests they are doing something.

Research by the psychologists Herbert Clark and Jean Fox Tree argued that fillers act as signals. Speakers use them to announce a coming delay while they plan what to say, and in English “uh” tends to signal a shorter pause than “um”. Listeners pick up on this: some studies suggest people pay closer attention to the next word after a filler, because they expect something less predictable to follow. In conversation, fillers can also hold your turn, telling others you have not finished.

So the goal is not to remove every filler but to reduce them where they distract, especially in formal speaking. The most effective substitute is a silent pause. A brief silence gives you the same planning time, sounds more deliberate and lets your previous point land. Practising pauses, rather than trying to suppress fillers by force, tends to work better, because the urge to fill silence fades once silence feels comfortable.
g: Fillers are treated as faults, but nearly everyone uses them in every language, suggesting they serve a purpose.
Clark and Fox Tree argued fillers signal upcoming delays and hold your turn, and listeners attend more closely after them.
So reduce distracting fillers by practising silent pauses, which give planning time and sound deliberate.
k: Fillers are universal, suggesting a function.
They signal delays (“uh” shorter than “um”), hold the turn, and can increase listener attention.

passages.q: Do bailouts encourage the risky behaviour that caused the crisis?
p: In 2008 governments in the United States, Britain and elsewhere spent enormous sums rescuing banks. Lehman Brothers was allowed to fail in September, and the chaos that followed convinced many policymakers that letting other large banks collapse would cause a depression. Banks deemed too big to fail received capital, guarantees and cheap loans.

Critics warned of moral hazard. If banks expect to be rescued when bets go wrong, they keep the profits in good times and pass losses to taxpayers in bad ones. That gives them reason to take more risk. Creditors who expect a bailout also lend more cheaply to big banks, giving them an advantage over smaller rivals and encouraging them to grow even larger.

Reforms since the crisis aim to reduce this problem. Banks must now hold much more capital to absorb losses, and many countries have created resolution regimes intended to let even large banks fail in an orderly way, with losses falling on shareholders and certain creditors rather than taxpayers. Whether these regimes would hold in a real panic remains untested at scale. The dilemma persists: rescues may be necessary to prevent disaster, yet expecting rescue can help create the next one.
g: In 2008 governments rescued big banks after Lehman’s collapse caused chaos, treating them as too big to fail.
Critics warned of moral hazard, because expected rescues let banks keep profits and pass losses on, encouraging risk and size.
Reforms require more capital and orderly failure plans, but they are untested, so the dilemma remains.
k: Governments rescued banks in 2008, fearing a depression after Lehman’s failure.
Moral hazard: expected rescues encourage risk-taking and cheaper funding for big banks.
More capital and resolution regimes aim to let banks fail safely; untested in a real panic.

passages.q: Why do some resource-rich countries grow slowly?
p: It might seem that discovering oil, gas or minerals would guarantee prosperity. Yet many resource-rich countries have grown more slowly than resource-poor ones and suffered more corruption and conflict. Economists call this pattern the resource curse.

Several mechanisms contribute. A resource boom raises the value of a country’s currency, making its other exports, such as manufactured goods, less competitive, a problem known as Dutch disease after the effect of gas discoveries on the Netherlands in the 1960s. Resource revenues are volatile, rising and falling with world prices, which makes planning difficult. And governments that can fund themselves from resource income rather than taxes may become less accountable to citizens, while control of the resources becomes a prize worth fighting over.

The curse is not inevitable. Norway, which discovered oil in 1969, placed much of its revenue in a sovereign wealth fund invested abroad, which has grown into one of the largest in the world. Spending only a small share of the fund each year protects the rest of the economy and saves wealth for future generations. Botswana has also managed diamond wealth relatively well. Strong institutions before the discovery seem to make the biggest difference.
g: Many resource-rich countries grow slowly and suffer corruption and conflict: the resource curse.
Causes include Dutch disease, volatile revenues and governments less accountable when not reliant on taxes.
It is not inevitable, as Norway’s fund and Botswana show, and strong prior institutions matter most.
k: Resource wealth often brings slow growth, corruption and conflict: the resource curse.
Dutch disease, volatile revenue and reduced accountability drive it.
Norway’s wealth fund and Botswana show it can be avoided; prior institutions matter most.

mc.e: The final paragraph gives this conclusion.

passages.q: Why did average IQ scores rise throughout the twentieth century?
p: IQ tests are designed so that the average score of a population is 100. To keep it there, tests are periodically re-normed against new samples. In the 1980s the political scientist James Flynn documented a striking fact: raw scores had been rising steadily in many countries, by about three points per decade. A person scoring average in 1950 would score below average against people tested decades later.

Genes cannot change that fast, so the cause must be environmental. Proposed explanations include better nutrition and health, smaller families, more years of schooling, and a world that increasingly demands abstract thinking. The largest gains appeared on tests of abstract reasoning, such as finding patterns in shapes, rather than on vocabulary or arithmetic. Flynn argued that people had not become more intelligent in every sense, but had learned to think in ways that modern life rewards, such as classifying things and reasoning about hypotheticals.

In some countries, including Norway and Denmark, the rise appears to have slowed or reversed since the 1990s, again for reasons that seem environmental. The Flynn effect carries a broader lesson: abilities measured by intelligence tests are shaped by the world people live in, which is why education and environment matter.

passages.q: How should companies balance long-term brand advertising with short-term sales campaigns?
p: Digital advertising made it easy to measure the immediate results of a campaign: clicks, sign-ups and sales within days. Many companies shifted budgets towards these performance campaigns, which produce visible, quick returns. Brand advertising, which builds memories and associations over months and years, became harder to justify in meetings that demanded proof.

The marketing researchers Les Binet and Peter Field analysed hundreds of campaigns from the IPA databank of advertising effectiveness. They found that short-term activation campaigns produce quick sales spikes that fade, while brand campaigns build slowly but produce larger, lasting growth, partly by reducing customers’ sensitivity to price. Their analysis suggested that, on average, many brands did best by spending around sixty per cent of budgets on brand building and forty on activation, though the ideal split varies by category and situation.

The work highlights a measurement trap. Because short-term effects are easy to count and long-term effects hard to see, organisations focused on quarterly numbers can drift towards tactics that look efficient now while eroding future growth. The lesson extends beyond marketing: what is easiest to measure is not always what matters most.

passages.q: What are the trade-offs behind fast fashion?
p: Fast fashion brands can move a design from sketch to shop in a matter of weeks, releasing new styles constantly at low prices. The model, pioneered by retailers such as Zara and pushed further by online sellers, gives customers variety and affordability that previous generations did not have. It has also made clothing a near-disposable product.

The costs are significant. Clothing production has grown enormously this century, while the number of times each garment is worn has fallen. Textile production uses large amounts of water and chemicals, and much discarded clothing ends up in landfill or is exported to countries that cannot absorb it. Low prices depend on low wages in supply chains, and the 2013 collapse of the Rana Plaza factory building in Bangladesh, which killed more than 1,100 workers, exposed how dangerous conditions could be.

Responses include stronger safety agreements, such as the accord signed after Rana Plaza, rules requiring brands to take responsibility for textile waste, and growing markets for second-hand and rented clothing. For individual buyers, the most effective change is often the simplest: buying fewer items and wearing them for longer, which reduces the impact of each garment more than recycling does.

passages.q: How did India build one of the world’s largest digital payment systems?
p: In 2016 India launched the Unified Payments Interface, or UPI, developed by the National Payments Corporation of India, an organisation set up by banks under the central bank’s guidance. UPI lets people send money instantly between bank accounts using a phone, often by scanning a QR code, with no fees for most ordinary transfers. Within a few years it was handling billions of transactions a month, from large purchases to a cup of tea at a roadside stall.

Several factors drove adoption. UPI was built as public infrastructure that any bank or app could connect to, so competing apps such as PhonePe, Google Pay and Paytm all used the same underlying network. It built on earlier foundations: a national digital identity system and a large push to open bank accounts. Cheap smartphones and mobile data spread rapidly, and the sudden withdrawal of high-value banknotes in November 2016 pushed many people towards digital payments.

UPI has drawn international attention as a model of digital public infrastructure, and several countries have explored linking to it. Challenges remain, including fraud targeting new users, concentration of most transactions in a few apps, and questions about how a system with near-zero fees will be funded over time. But it has changed how hundreds of millions of people and small businesses handle money.

passages.q: Why do economists worry about falling prices?
p: Falling prices sound like good news for shoppers. Technology often gets cheaper, which no one regrets. But economists distinguish this from deflation: a general, sustained fall in prices across the economy. Central banks fear deflation almost as much as high inflation.

Deflation can feed on itself. If people expect prices to keep falling, they may delay purchases, reducing demand and pushing prices down further. Firms facing falling prices may cut wages or jobs. Debts become heavier in real terms, because borrowers must repay fixed amounts with money that is worth more, while their incomes may be falling. And central banks find it hard to fight deflation, since interest rates cannot easily go far below zero.

Japan experienced long periods of mild deflation and very low inflation from the late 1990s, alongside slow growth, in what became known as its lost decades. Economists debate how much deflation itself caused the stagnation, as opposed to an ageing population and the aftermath of a property bubble. But Japan’s experience is one reason central banks target low positive inflation, typically around two per cent, rather than zero: it leaves a buffer against slipping into deflation.
g: Cheaper goods are welcome, but general sustained falling prices, deflation, worry central banks.
Deflation can feed on itself through delayed spending, wage cuts, heavier debts and limits on interest rates.

passages.q: Is it acceptable for governments to steer choices without people noticing?
p: In their 2008 book Nudge, Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein argued for “libertarian paternalism”: designing choices to steer people towards better outcomes, such as saving more or eating healthily, while leaving them free to choose otherwise. Placing fruit at eye level or making pension saving the default changes behaviour without banning anything. Governments created nudge units to apply the ideas.

Critics raise several concerns. Nudges often work because people do not notice them, which can feel manipulative, especially when used by powerful institutions. Who decides what counts as a better outcome? A nudge designed for one group’s good may not fit people with different values or circumstances. Some argue that nudges can be a cheap substitute for harder policies, such as regulation or taxes, that would address problems more directly. And evidence reviews have suggested that the average effect of nudges in published studies may be smaller than early enthusiasm implied once publication bias is considered.

Defenders reply that choice architecture is unavoidable: every form, menu and website has some default, so the question is not whether to influence choices but how. Sunstein has proposed tests such as transparency: a nudge is more legitimate if it would still be acceptable when openly disclosed. The debate continues over where helpful design ends and manipulation begins.
g: Thaler and Sunstein proposed nudges that steer choices while preserving freedom, and governments adopted them.

passages.t: Why airlines sell more seats than they have
passages.q: Is overbooking flights a reasonable practice?
p: Airlines routinely sell more tickets than there are seats on a flight. This sounds unfair, but it reflects a predictable fact: on most flights a certain share of passengers do not turn up. Business travellers change plans, connections are missed and some people simply forget. An empty seat at departure is revenue lost for ever.

Using data on past flights, airlines estimate how many passengers are likely to be no-shows and sell tickets accordingly. Most of the time, the numbers work out and everyone who arrives gets a seat, while fewer seats fly empty. This keeps average fares lower than they would otherwise be. When too many passengers do arrive, airlines must find volunteers to take a later flight, usually by offering compensation that rises until enough people accept.

The practice becomes unfair when it is handled badly. In 2017 a passenger was forcibly removed from an overbooked United Airlines flight, causing public outrage and prompting changes to policies, including larger offers to volunteers. Regulations in the EU and elsewhere set minimum compensation for passengers denied boarding. Overbooking illustrates a common business trade-off: a statistically sound practice can still damage trust if its rare failures are handled without care.

passages.q: How do countries trade water without shipping any?
p: A kilogram of wheat requires roughly a thousand litres or more of water to grow, and a kilogram of beef many times that. When a country imports food, it is effectively importing the water used to produce it. The geographer John Anthony Allan called this embedded water “virtual water”, and he received the Stockholm Water Prize in 2008 for the idea.

Virtual water helps explain how water-scarce countries feed themselves. Many countries in the Middle East and North Africa import large amounts of grain, saving their limited water for drinking, industry and higher-value crops. In effect, rain falling on farms in other continents supplies their diets. Allan argued that this trade quietly prevented conflicts over water, because importing food was far cheaper than fighting over rivers.

The concept also reveals hidden pressures. Some countries with serious water stress export water-intensive crops, using up groundwater to grow produce sold abroad. California’s almonds and some Indian rice exports have drawn attention for this reason. Virtual water does not mean all trade in thirsty crops is wrong, since growing food where water is plentiful can be efficient. But it shows that water decisions are made in supermarket aisles as well as at reservoirs.

passages.q: How sustainable is the free, open-source software the world relies on?
p: Much of the world’s digital infrastructure runs on open-source software: code that anyone can use, inspect and modify for free. Operating systems, web servers, encryption libraries and countless smaller tools are maintained by communities of volunteers and companies. The model has been remarkably successful, allowing knowledge to accumulate and spreading the cost of maintenance across many users.

Its weak point became visible in 2014 with Heartbleed, a serious security flaw in OpenSSL, a library used to encrypt a large share of web traffic. It emerged that OpenSSL, despite its importance, had been maintained by a very small team with tiny funding. In 2021 a flaw in Log4j, a widely used logging tool maintained by volunteers, forced companies around the world into emergency fixes. Critical pieces of software often rest on a handful of people working in their spare time.

Responses include industry funds that pay maintainers, companies assigning staff to projects they depend on, and governments treating open-source security as part of national infrastructure. The underlying problem is a classic one: everyone benefits from well-maintained shared code, but each user is tempted to let others pay. Like a public park, open source thrives only if someone tends it.

Heartbleed and Log4j showed critical code often rests on tiny, underfunded volunteer teams.
Funds, company staff and government support are responses, because shared code suffers when everyone lets others pay.

passages.q: Why do deposit return schemes recover so many bottles?
p: In a deposit return scheme, buyers pay a small extra charge on drinks containers, which they get back when they return the empty bottle or can. Germany introduced a deposit on many single-use containers in 2003, now set at 25 cents. Return rates for these containers are reported at around ninety-eight per cent, far higher than for typical household recycling.

The schemes work by giving each container a value. A bottle thrown away is money thrown away, so most people return them, and those who do not create an incentive for others to collect them. Returned containers are clean and sorted by type, which makes them much easier to recycle into new bottles than mixed household waste. Shops are often required to take containers back, so returning them fits into ordinary shopping trips.

Deposit schemes are not free to run. Collection machines, logistics and administration cost money, and retailers must give up space. Critics argue that kerbside recycling, if improved, could achieve similar results more cheaply. But many countries, including Scotland, Ireland and others, have introduced or planned deposit schemes, drawn by evidence that putting a price on a bottle changes behaviour more reliably than appeals to good intentions.

passages.t: The camera Kodak invented and ignored
passages.q: Why do successful companies miss technologies they themselves invent?
p: In 1975 Steven Sasson, an engineer at Eastman Kodak, built one of the first digital cameras. It weighed several kilograms and took around twenty seconds to record a low-resolution image to a cassette tape. Kodak dominated photographic film, earning large profits on every roll sold and developed.

Kodak did not ignore digital photography completely; it continued research and later sold digital cameras. But the company’s profits and identity were built on film, and digital threatened to destroy that business. Managers faced a dilemma familiar in many industries: investing heavily in a new technology would cannibalise the profitable old one, while the new market was initially small and less profitable. Moving slowly seemed rational at each step.

By the 2000s, digital cameras and then smartphones had made film a niche product, and Kodak filed for bankruptcy protection in 2012. The case is often used to illustrate the innovator’s dilemma, a term popularised by Clayton Christensen: well-run companies, listening carefully to their best customers and protecting margins, can be overtaken by technologies that start out inferior but improve rapidly. Seeing a threat is not the same as being willing to act on it.
g: Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built an early digital camera in 1975 while Kodak profited hugely from film.

passages.t: Why we love what we build
passages.q: Why do people overvalue things they have made themselves?
p: In a set of experiments published in 2012, the researchers Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely asked people to assemble simple IKEA storage boxes, fold origami or build Lego models. Participants were then asked how much they would pay for their creations. They valued their own work far more highly than identical items assembled by others, and they expected other people to share their high opinion.

The researchers called this the IKEA effect. Labour seems to increase love, but only when the effort succeeds: people who built something and then had it destroyed, or who failed to finish, did not show the same boost. The effect may stem from a need to feel competent and from the meaning we attach to our own effort.

The finding helps explain why customers value products they customise and why companies can benefit from letting users take part in creation. It also carries a warning for leaders and teams. People can overvalue their own ideas, strategies and code simply because they built them, making it harder to abandon a flawed plan or accept a better idea from outside. Recognising the pull of effort is a first step towards judging work on its merits.
